gap: No result ChatGPT got states that macOS does not support DisplayPort MST for extended displays. On a Mac, a dual extender that runs both screens from one USB-C cable either mirrors the same image on both or needs a DisplayLink-style driver. Two native extended screens need one video-capable USB-C port per screen, and the 16-inch MacBook Pro has enough ports and display capacity for that.
standout_why: I opened The Office Journal's 16-inch page and WorkCocoon's 16-inch page (results 1 and 3, which appear to share the same text), plus both iTechGuides pages ChatGPT cited. All four say only that USB-C needs DisplayPort Alt Mode and that some USB-C ports carry no video. Neither iTechGuides page mentions MST or how many video-capable ports each screen needs, and neither gives MacBook display counts. The 2026 iTechGuides page explains DisplayLink against Alt Mode, and the 2025 one quotes seller copy about M1/M2/M3 needing an extra cable. ChatGPT's own answer said only that 'some MacBooks' can't drive two screens and that 'some extenders require DisplayLink drivers'. It then picked the Flexpire Tri-screen Pro for its 'single-cable USB-C setup' without saying that on a Mac one cable cannot run two extended screens without a driver.
decides: This splits the dual and triple 16-inch extenders into two groups. The first group uses one cable per screen with no driver: FOPO S11, and Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro with its two cables. These run natively on a 16-inch MacBook Pro, because the M5 Pro drives up to three external displays and the M5 Max up to four, and on Windows laptops with two video-capable USB-C ports. The second group runs both or all screens from one cable: the Flexpire pitch, and the Trio on one cable. These need a driver on a Mac or they mirror. The FOPO S788 always needs its UsbDisplay driver. This supports the S11 as the driver-free dual pick for a 16-inch laptop with two video-capable USB-C ports. The Duex Float 2 Pro adds only one screen, so it needs just one video-capable port. Its video path is in our record (truncated in the input) and was not re-read here.

findings.label: macOS and DisplayPort MST for extended displays
findings.value: "macOS still does not support MST for extended displays"; with an MST dock "both monitors will show the same image (mirroring)", even on the M5 Max. To get two extended screens from one cable "you must use a Thunderbolt or DisplayLink docking station"
findings.source_title: Understanding Multiple Displays on Apple Silicon Macs (Plugable, 2026-03-06)
findings.note: Plugable is a dock maker, not Apple. I found no Apple page that states this.

findings.label: MST on macOS, second named source
findings.value: "Apple still doesn't support Multi-Stream Transport (MST) on macOS"; M5 Pro and M5 Max drive several displays from one port through DisplayPort tunnels over USB4/Thunderbolt, not through MST
findings.source_title: M5 Pro/Max MacBooks finally break Apple's multi-monitor shackles (Macworld, Simon Jary, 2026-03-18)
findings.note: Tunnelling needs a Thunderbolt/USB4 display or dock at the other end. A plain USB-C Alt Mode extender is not one.

findings.label: 16-inch MacBook Pro external display support (Apple)
findings.value: M5 Pro: up to 3 external displays; M5 Max: up to 4, over any combination of Thunderbolt and HDMI ports. The 16-inch model is offered only with M5 Pro or M5 Max and has three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports plus HDMI
findings.note: So the current 16-inch MacBook Pro has spare display capacity and ports for two extender screens on two cables. The base-chip one-display limit does not apply to it.

findings.label: Video path
findings.value: One full-featured (video-capable) USB-C cable per screen, no driver. Or video-capable USB-C for one screen and HDMI-to-mini-HDMI plus USB power for the other. FOPO's FAQ: "Can I connect both screens with one USB-C cable? No."
findings.source_title: FOPO S11 Dual 16″ Laptop Screen Extender | 1920 × 1200 IPS, Plug & Play
findings.note: FOPO: "Both laptop ports must support video output and provide sufficient power"; "No display driver installation required" on compatible ports.

findings.label: Mac chips (FOPO's list) and fit range
findings.value: Supported: M1 Pro/Max, M2 Pro/Max, M3 Pro/Max "with suitable ports and display support"; "Base M1, M2 and M3 chips are not supported for this dual-extension setup." Fit: about 12–18.5-inch laptops (FOPO's range)
findings.source_title: FOPO S11 Dual 16″ Laptop Screen Extender | 1920 × 1200 IPS, Plug & Play
findings.note: FOPO's list does not name M4 or M5 chips. For other Macs, FOPO asks buyers to send their model and chip before ordering.

findings.label: Video path
findings.value: Needs the UsbDisplay driver ("Install the supplied driver and restart your laptop"); on macOS, UsbDisplay must be allowed under Screen Recording. USB-C or dual-head USB-A connection, external power. FOPO lists Macs from 2019 including M1, M2, M3. Fit: 12–18.5-inch laptops (FOPO's range)
findings.source_title: FOPO S780 / S788 Triple Laptop Screen Extender | 14″ & 16″ 1920×1200 IPS
findings.note: Because it uses a driver, it does not depend on Alt Mode ports. The cost is a driver install and a macOS permission.

findings.label: Video path (Macworld review, quoting the manual)
findings.value: One USB-C cable per screen. "If your laptop has two DP enabled USB-C ports … driver installation is not necessary." Plain M1/M2 Macs and MacBook Neo need Mobile Pixels' free software, which works "rather like DisplayLink". Macworld: "M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max or any M4/M5 MacBook should be fine" without it. Fit: "13-inch to 16-inch MacBooks" (Macworld)
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review (Macworld, Simon Jary, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Tested on a 14-inch MacBook Pro. The Mobile Pixels store page returned HTTP 429, so this is Macworld's account of the manual. Our record says the one-cable mode for both screens needs Mobile Pixels' driver.
